newsitem.title: USA: White soldier's trial for killing two blacks opens.
newsitem.headline: White soldier's trial for killing two blacks opens.

text.p: A former private in the U.S. Army's elite 82nd Airborne Division was portrayed as "pure unmitigated evil" at the start of his murder trial Tuesday for the racially motivated killings of two blacks.
James Burmeister, 21, a white who has been linked to a Skinhead hate group, was charged with shooting Jackie Burden and Michael James as they walked through Fayetteville on Dec. 7, 1995.

In his 10-minute opening statement Prosecutor John Dickson told the jury in a soft voice that the former soldier from Fort Bragg, North Carolina, murdered the man and woman only because they were black.
"Jackie Burden and Michael James weren't doing anything wrong or illegal, just walking," Dickson said. Pointing at Burmeister he declared: "The evidence will speak for itself and speak strongly."

He told jurors Burmeister had a jacket with a German iron cross on it, a backwards American flag with a yellow border, and a pierced nipple -- all part of his life as an alleged racist Skinhead that culminated in the murder of the two.

But defence attorney Carl Ivarsson told jurors to reject the race issue. He said the case was not about world history, the 1930s and '40s, Hitler, the Nazis or Skinheads. "It's only about the guilt or innocence of Jim Burmeister."

The prosecution plans to seek the death penalty if a guilty verdict is returned in the first-degree murder trial of Burmeister, who is from Thompson, Pennsylvania. The state's key witness is Randy Meadows, another former member of 82nd Airborne accused of driving Burmeister and another white soldier to the area where the killings occurred.

Meadows, 22, of Lexington, Kentucky, pleaded guilty to assault charges in exchange for his testimony against Burmeister, defence attorneys said. Meadows could have faced 64 years in prison but the plea bargain was likely to reduce that time to 21 years, Ivarsson said.
Malcolm Wright, 22, the other former private charged in the shooting deaths, was scheduled to go on trial March 31.
Court records and police reports say the soldiers left a bar to search for blacks or drug dealers to attack and spotted James and Burden walking along a street.
Burmeister and Wright got out of the car and Meadows, waiting in the car for them to return, heard six gunshots. James was shot in the head, while Burden died from bullet wounds to her head and back.

Burmeister and Wright never returned to the car, choosing instead to take a cab back to Burmeister's trailer. Meadows was arrested minutes after the shooting when a police officer saw him sitting in the car.

He gave police a statement that night and police said he told them Burmeister wanted to earn a spider web tattoo, a Skinhead symbol police say represents the killing of a homosexual or a black person.
Police found white-supremacist literature, a Nazi flag and a book on how to make a bomb in Burmeister's trailer home.
